images.alt: Puri beach on the Bay of Bengal

overview.text:
Puri, on the Bay of Bengal, is one of the four Char Dhams of Hindu pilgrimage and appears in ancient texts as Purushottama Kshetra. Its heart is the 12th-century Jagannath Temple, where a family has climbed the spire barefoot to change the flag every day for over eight centuries, and where the kitchen, said to be the second largest in the world, cooks the Mahaprasad. Entry to the temple is for Hindus only.

The great festival is the Rath Yatra each June or July, when the deities ride huge chariots through town; Snana Yatra, Chandan Yatra and Kartik Purnima are celebrated too. Beyond the temple are a long beach, Odissi dance, sand sculptures, Pattachitra paintings and seafood. The Konark Sun Temple is about 35 km away. October to February is the most comfortable time.

places.name: Konark Sun Temple
places.summary: A 13th-century temple built as the Sun God's chariot, 35 km from Puri — a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.seoTitle: Konark Sun Temple: History, Wheels & Visiting Hours
places.seoDescription: Konark Sun Temple: a 13th-century chariot of the Sun God with 24 carved wheels, 35 km from Puri, UNESCO-listed in 1984; open 6 am–8 pm.

overview.text:
The Konark Sun Temple, about 35 km north-east of Puri, was built around 1250 CE by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty as a giant stone chariot for the Sun God, with 24 carved wheels. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda, and it once stood at the mouth of the Chandrabhaga river before the sea receded.

The main tower, once an estimated 227 ft, has fallen; the jagamohana (audience hall), about 39 m tall, is the principal surviving structure. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984 and appears on the ₹10 note. Fallen sculptures are in the ASI museum next door. The temple is open from 6 am to 8 pm.
